from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section1Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Prerequisite: Defining the Planar Graph", [
            "Planar graphs avoid edge crossings.", 
            "Vertices, edges, and faces define structure.", 
            "Faces include the outer infinite region."
        ])
        
        # Create a simple planar graph (Square with diagonals, 4 nodes)
        nodes = VGroup(*[Dot(color=WHITE) for _ in range(4)])
        edges = VGroup(
            Line(nodes[0], nodes[1], color=WHITE),
            Line(nodes[1], nodes[2], color=WHITE),
            Line(nodes[2], nodes[3], color=WHITE),
            Line(nodes[3], nodes[0], color=WHITE)
        )
        
        self.place_at_grid(nodes[0], "B2")
        self.place_at_grid(nodes[1], "B4")
        self.place_at_grid(nodes[2], "D4")
        self.place_at_grid(nodes[3], "D2")
        
        graph = VGroup(edges, nodes)
        self.add(graph)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color(YELLOW)
        self.play(FadeIn(graph))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.lecture[1].set_color(YELLOW)
        self.play(
            nodes.animate.set_color("#FF5733"),
            run_time=2
        )
        self.play(
            nodes.animate.set_color(WHITE),
            run_time=2
        )

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.lecture[2].set_color(YELLOW)
        self.play(
            edges.animate.set_color("#33FF57"),
            run_time=2
        )
        self.play(
            edges.animate.set_color(WHITE),
            run_time=2
        )

class Section2Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "Euler's formula links graph components.",
            "V minus E plus F equals 2.",
            "Moving vertices preserves this constant value."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("Euler\u2019s Characteristic Formula (V - E + F = 2)", lecture_lines)
        
        # Formula setup
        formula = MathTex(r"V", "-", r"E", "+", r"F", "=", "2")
        self.place_at_grid(formula, 'C3', scale_factor=1.5)
        
        v_part = formula[0]
        e_part = formula[2]
        f_part = formula[4]
        res_part = formula[6]
        
        # Labels
        lbl_v = Text("Vertices", font_size=20, color="#FF5733")
        lbl_e = Text("Edges", font_size=20, color="#33FF57")
        lbl_f = Text("Faces", font_size=20, color="#3357FF")
        
        self.place_at_grid(lbl_v, 'B2', scale_factor=0.8)
        self.place_at_grid(lbl_e, 'D2', scale_factor=0.8)
        self.place_at_grid(lbl_f, 'B4', scale_factor=0.8)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(YELLOW))
        self.play(Write(formula))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(YELLOW))
        self.play(
            v_part.animate.set_color("#FF5733"),
            e_part.animate.set_color("#33FF57"),
            f_part.animate.set_color("#3357FF"),
            FadeIn(lbl_v), FadeIn(lbl_e), FadeIn(lbl_f)
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(YELLOW))
        self.play(res_part.animate.set_color(WHITE).set_opacity(0.5))
        self.play(Flash(res_part, color=WHITE, line_length=0.2, num_lines=15))
        self.wait(2)

class Section3Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("The Concept of Graph Duality", [
            "Dual graphs represent face connectivity.",
            "Place nodes inside each original face.",
            "Connect nodes sharing original edges."
        ])

        # Define G (the original graph)
        # Vertices and edges
        v_coords = {
            "v1": self.grid["B3"],
            "v2": self.grid["C2"],
            "v3": self.grid["C4"],
            "v4": self.grid["D3"]
        }
        
        g_vertices = VGroup(*[Dot(v_coords[v], color=WHITE) for v in v_coords])
        g_edges = VGroup(
            Line(v_coords["v1"], v_coords["v2"], color=WHITE),
            Line(v_coords["v1"], v_coords["v3"], color=WHITE),
            Line(v_coords["v2"], v_coords["v4"], color=WHITE),
            Line(v_coords["v3"], v_coords["v4"], color=WHITE)
        )
        graph = VGroup(g_vertices, g_edges)

        # Dual Vertices (inside faces)
        # Face 1: Left
        dv1 = Dot(self.grid["C3"], color="#FFC300")
        # Face 2: Right (outside)
        dv2 = Dot(self.grid["D5"], color="#FFC300")
        
        dual_vertices = VGroup(dv1, dv2)
        dual_edges = VGroup(
            Line(dv1.get_center(), dv2.get_center(), color="#FFC300", stroke_width=4)
        )

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(FadeIn(graph))
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#FFC300")
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(FadeIn(dual_vertices))
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#FFC300")
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(FadeIn(dual_edges))
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#FFC300")
        self.wait(2)

class Section4Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Properties and Mapping", [
            "Faces become vertices, vertices become faces.",
            "Duality simplifies complex topological problems.",
            "Mapped interactions minimize design interference."
        ])
        
        # Visualization assets
        # A simple planar graph representation
        v1 = Dot(color=WHITE)
        v2 = Dot(color=WHITE)
        v3 = Dot(color=WHITE)
        self.place_at_grid(v1, 'B2')
        self.place_at_grid(v2, 'B4')
        self.place_at_grid(v3, 'D3')
        
        edges = VGroup(
            Line(v1.get_center(), v2.get_center(), color=WHITE),
            Line(v2.get_center(), v3.get_center(), color=WHITE),
            Line(v3.get_center(), v1.get_center(), color=WHITE)
        )
        self.add(edges, v1, v2, v3)

        # Dual graph elements
        dv = Dot(color="#FF5733")
        self.place_at_grid(dv, 'C3')
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color("#FFD700"))
        # Show mapping of faces to vertices with color-coded arrows
        arrow = Arrow(start=self.grid['C3'], end=self.grid['C3'], color="#FFFFFF") # placeholder for mapping
        self.add(arrow)
        self.play(FadeIn(dv))
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color("#00FF00"))
        # Highlight one face and its dual vertex
        face_highlight = Circle(radius=0.3, color="#FF5733", fill_opacity=0.3)
        self.place_at_grid(face_highlight, 'C3')
        self.play(Create(face_highlight))
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color("#00BFFF"))
        # Demonstrate edge correspondence
        edge_dual = Line(self.grid['C3'], self.grid['C3'], color="#FF5733")
        self.play(Create(edge_dual))
        self.wait(1)

class Section5Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Synthesis and Summary", ["Euler balances graph geometry.", "Duality mirrors the structure.", "Essential for modern network optimization."])
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        euler = MathTex(r"V - E + F = 2", color=WHITE)
        self.place_in_area(euler, "B2", "C5")
        self.play(Write(euler))
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(BLUE))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Simple representation of duality: original graph (cube-like) and dual

        square = Square(color=YELLOW)
        dual_diamond = RegularPolygon(n=4, start_angle=45*DEGREES, color=RED)
        
        dual_group = VGroup(square, dual_diamond)
        self.place_in_area(dual_group, "D2", "E5")
        self.play(Create(square), Create(dual_diamond))
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(GREEN))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Fade everything except formula
        self.play(
            FadeOut(square),
            FadeOut(dual_diamond),
            self.lecture[0].animate.set_color("#808080"),
            self.lecture[1].animate.set_color("#808080"),
            self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(ORANGE),

        self.wait(2)

sections.title: Prerequisite: Defining the Planar Graph
sections.content: Define a planar graph as a graph that can be drawn in a 2D plane without edges crossing. Introduce the basic components: Vertices (V), Edges (E), and Faces (F), where a face is an enclosed region (including the infinite outer region).
sections.example: Visualizing a house shape: 5 vertices, 6 edges, 2 enclosed faces + 1 outer face = 3 total faces.

sections.title: Euler’s Characteristic Formula (V - E + F = 2)
sections.content: Introduce the fundamental theorem for connected planar graphs. Explain that for any such graph, the number of vertices minus edges plus faces always equals 2. Show a quick animation where moving a vertex preserves this constant.
sections.example: A simple triangle (V=3, E=3, F=2) satisfies 3 - 3 + 2 = 2.

sections.title: The Concept of Graph Duality
sections.content: Define the 'Dual Graph' (G*): Place a node in the center of every face of the original graph. Connect two nodes if their corresponding faces share an edge. Explain the inversion: Vertices of G become faces of G*, and vice versa.
sections.example: Imagine a network of rooms (faces) in a maze; the dual graph represents the 'pathway' nodes connected by doors (shared edges).

sections.title: Properties and Mapping
sections.content: Highlight the inverse relationship: V* = F and F* = V. Explain that duality helps solve complex topological problems by transforming a graph into a structurally simpler or more intuitive dual representation.
sections.example: Map a complex circuit board layout (Graph) to its component interaction map (Dual Graph) to minimize signal interference.

sections.title: Synthesis and Summary
sections.content: Briefly recap how Euler's formula provides the 'balance' of the graph, while duality provides the 'mirror' view. Conclude that these tools are essential for VLSI design, cartography, and network optimization.
sections.example: Summarize with an animation of a cube (planar projection) transforming into its dual (octahedron vertices) to solidify the concept of geometric duality.
